title: Was Miyamoto Musashi Late on Purpose? A Stone From 9 Years After His Death Doesn't Name His Rival
description:
On Ganryūjima, Kojirō waited over two hours before Musashi rowed in, his wooden sword carved from an oar, late on purpose. Manga, TV and games all show it; in 2003 Musashi's bronze statue was unveiled four months after Kojirō's, and the island's official guide leaflet joked that maybe it matched the "historical fact" that he was late to the duel. Yet the record closest to that day doesn't even name his opponent.

This episode reads the testimony in the order the witnesses spoke: the stone Musashi's adopted son Miyamoto Iori raised in Kokura in Jōō 3 (1654), nine years after his death, which says "the two heroes met at the same time" and calls the opponent only "Ganryū"; the record of the Numata, castle wardens of Moji, which calls him only "Kojirō"; a Kokura merchant who in Shōtoku 2 (1712) passed on the boatman's words, written up by three Toyoda generations in Kumamoto as the Bukōden of Hōreki 5 (1755) and the Nitenki of An'ei 5 (1776), with the disappearance, the letter, the oversleeping, the carved oar, "Are you late?", "Kojirō has lost" and "said to be eighteen," but never why he arrived late; in Meiji 42 (1909) the Miyamoto Musashi memorial society in Kumamoto laid the accounts side by side, chose the Nitenki, adding a few lines in the retelling; the earliest text we found calling the lateness a ploy is a short story by Naoki Sanjūgo (d. 1934), who also recorded a criticism of unknown origin; and Yoshikawa Eiji's Musashi (Asahi Shimbun serial, 1935–1939) made it famous. Last, The Book of Five Rings, which Musashi himself began in Kan'ei 20 (1643).

For the Nitenki we used volume 2 of the Higo Bunken Sōsho, and the memorial society's Miyamoto Musashi (which quotes the Kokura stone, The Book of Five Rings and the Numata Kaki); both are in the National Diet Library Digital Collections. Naoki Sanjūgo's "Ganryūjima" and Yoshikawa Eiji's novel and essays are from Aozora Bunko. We did not open the original Numata Kaki, only its quotes in the society's book; The Book of Five Rings is the copy printed there. The Nitenki dates the duel to the fourth month of Keichō 17 (1612); another account puts it over ten years earlier.

Every quotation, year and number is sourced in the references below. Dates in the narration follow the old lunar calendar, and sentences beginning "we think" or "my thought here" are this channel's view. The leaflet is quoted as text only, no screenshot.

This episode's illustrations are AI-generated. Historical figures are unnamed cartoon characters not meant to resemble anyone; Yoshikawa Eiji, Naoki Sanjūgo and modern researchers are not drawn.

Information as of 2026-10-19 (rewritten under new rules on 2026-10-25)

mv101.text: You've seen it: Kojirō waits over two hours on Ganryūjima, then Musashi rows in, his wooden sword carved from an oar.

mv102.text: Those two-plus hours decide who your Musashi is: a strategist who timed it, or a man of petty tricks.

mv103.text: In 2003, Musashi's bronze statue on the island was unveiled, four months after Kojirō's.

mv104.text: The guide joked: maybe to fit the "fact" he was late.

mv105.text: I dug in. The earliest record: a stone his son raised nine years after he died.

mv107.text: Stranger still, in 1909, someone in Kumamoto laid every version out on one table.

mv108.text: This file opens the four testimonies about that day, one by one.

mv109.text: That day, was he late on purpose or not?

mv201.text: In the fourth month of 1654, it went up below Kokura Castle.

mv202.text: It was raised by Musashi's adopted son, Miyamoto Iori.

mv203.text: The stone says a devoted son raised it for posterity.

mv204.text: The first witness, and the one keenest to defend him.

mv205.text: It first praises him: over sixty bouts, never once beaten. Remember that number.

mv206.text: His rival? As I said, the stone gives no name, just "Ganryū," a master swordsman.

mv208.text: Musashi replied: you use steel, I'll use wood.

mv209.text: Then both came ashore. What does the stone say?

mv210.text: "The two heroes met at the same time." Both arrived together.

mv211.text: This earliest testimony never mentions lateness;

mv212.text: though "at the same time" may just mean both showed up, not to the minute.

mv213.text: My thought here: as the son raising it, even if your father was late, you'd hardly carve that.

mv214.text: The result is brief: one wooden-sword blow; even lightning was slower.

mv215.text: From then on, Funashima was called Ganryūjima.

mv216.text: But were they alone on the island?

mv217.text: Another is the Numata Kaki, of Moji's castle wardens.

mv218.text: As far as we found, the name "Kojirō" first appears here.

mv219.text: It began with their students arguing whose sword style was stronger.

mv220.text: It says Musashi didn't strike alone at the end; known only secondhand, that's still disputed.

mv221.text: Strange. Then where did the lateness story come from?

mv301.text: The record says most details came from an old boatman.

mv302.text: The book notes the elder Okinaga handled it, and his family passed it down;

mv303.text: the boatman is a separate line.

mv304.text: In spring 1712, a full century after the duel, a merchant came from Kokura to Yatsushiro in Higo.

mv305.text: A samurai, Toyoda Masakata, asked him: what really happened on Ganryūjima?

mv306.text: As a young man, Masakata had heard Musashi's late-life students talk of him; now he asked about that day.

mv307.text: He said a relative ran a Shimonoseki wholesaler where Musashi stayed;

mv308.text: an old man there had rowed Musashi's boat that day.

mv310.text: No. The book says he came many times, and told it word for word each time.

mv311.text: Word for word, every time. Reading that, I felt uneasy; you may too.

mv312.text: Three generations of the Toyoda family made it a book: in 1755, the Bukōden;

mv313.text: in 1776, a grandson renamed it the Nitenki.

mv314.text: From that day to this book: 164 years.

mv315.text: Its notes admit: Musashi fought dozens of bouts, and the many stories often get mixed up.

mv316.text: This family trained in Musashi's own school.

mv317.text: How did they write that day?

mv401.text: It says in the fourth month of 1612, Musashi came from Kyoto to Kokura.

mv402.text: Kojirō, it says, was from Echizen and founded the Ganryū style; lord Hosokawa Tadaoki had him teach in Kokura.

mv403.text: An elder set it: Ganryū Kojirō, the island, as the Dragon hour opens tomorrow.

mv404.text: The Dragon hour, on your watch, is roughly 7 to 9 a.m.

mv405.text: Inspectors kept watch under strict orders.

mv408.text: You're in town; the night before the bout, he's gone. What would you think?

mv409.text: Word in town: he got scared and ran.

mv410.text: He was later found in Shimonoseki, at the boatman's wholesaler.

mv411.text: The book also has a letter said to be his: he won't take the elder's boat; he'll sail from here himself.

mv412.text: The reason is polite: Kojirō rides the lord's boat; if I took the elder's, how would that look to the lord?

mv413.text: As the elder reading this, you'd want to know one thing: when is he coming?

mv414.text: The letter says only: when the time is right, I'll come over.

mv501.text: Next day, the hour neared. And Musashi?

mv502.text: The sun was high, and he was still asleep.

mv503.text: Kokura's runner came twice to hurry him. "Right away," he said, then washed his face and ate.

mv504.text: Remember the wooden weapon on the stone? Here, it gets a backstory:

mv505.text: He asked the innkeeper for an oar and carved it ashore into a big wooden sword.

mv506.text: He landed in the Snake hour or later; that's where those two-plus hours come from.

mv508.text: At the shore he yelled: "I came early! Are you late?!"

mv509.text: He drew his 3-foot-plus sword and threw the scabbard to sea.

mv511.text: "Kojirō, you've lost. Would a winner throw away his scabbard?"

mv512.text: The book says Kojirō's stroke cut through Musashi's headband; it was that close.

mv513.text: Done: Kojirō lost. Musashi bowed to the inspectors and took his boat back to Shimonoseki.

mv514.text: The book adds that some faulted Musashi for leaving so fast; he replied: with orders that strict, you can guess.

mv515.text: The rival unnamed on the stone gets a full name by the end: Sasaki Kojirō,

mv516.text: eighteen then, though the book only says "it is said."

mv517.text: Did you notice? For all that detail, one thing is missing: why he arrived late.

mv518.text: So where were the words "on purpose" first written down?

mv601.text: Before that was written, the table from the start stepped in.

mv602.text: Kumamoto's Musashi memorial society was compiling Miyamoto Musashi.

mv603.text: The Numata say more than one struck at the end? The editors: not credible.

mv604.text: Remember the inspectors? The editors' reason: orders that strict made it impossible.

mv605.text: But the reason is the Nitenki's own: Musashi's reply from earlier.

mv606.text: Their verdict: for now, follow the Nitenki.

mv607.text: But did they believe all of it?

mv608.text: And that "said to be eighteen" at the end? The editors admit the Nitenki's ages are unreliable.

mv609.text: They add that in Edo-era plays, Kojirō was actually the elder and Musashi the young one.

mv610.text: Your young Kojirō was the other way round on the Edo stage.

mv611.text: An editor even crossed the sea to look for Kojirō's grave, and found no trace.

mv612.text: The next year, a "Sasaki Ganryū Monument" rose mid-island; it's the one you'll see there today.

mv613.text: Stranger still, retelling that Nitenki passage, they added lines.

mv614.text: When the runner comes, this book says Kojirō is already there.

mv615.text: And Musashi? He slowly rose, calmly got to his feet, and put on a lined silk robe.

mv616.text: Kojirō's "Are you late?" became: "You broke our pact. Outrageous!"

mv617.text: None of these lines is in the Nitenki itself.

mv618.text: We think by now, arriving late starts to look like an attitude.

mv619.text: The tone is there. But the motive?

mv701.text: The first to write him a motive, as far as we found, was a short story by Naoki Sanjūgo, who died in 1934.

mv702.text: He followed the Nitenki, calling it reliable.

mv703.text: He wrote that even asleep, Musashi seemed to be plotting against Kojirō.

mv704.text: Then he quotes a criticism already going around: stalling on purpose to wear the rival down is a cowardly trick.

mv705.text: Who said it, and how early, we haven't found; Naoki himself says it may be a later voice.

mv706.text: Then he defends Musashi: in most bouts he came a little late, on purpose, to rattle his rivals.

mv707.text: Critics call it cowardly, defenders call it strategy; both say it was deliberate.

mv708.text: So the answer to that question: in writing that survives, this is the earliest "on purpose" we found.

mv709.text: A year-plus after Naoki died, Yoshikawa Eiji's Musashi began in the Asahi Shimbun, running four years.

mv710.text: First on Yoshikawa's own list of sources: the Kumamoto society's Miyamoto Musashi.

mv712.text: Yoshikawa's essay calls it the most reliable;

mv713.text: he even faulted the stone: nearest Musashi's life, yet flawed, of little documentary value.

mv714.text: And he said Musashi's first move against Kojirō was to break the set time on purpose.

mv715.text: The novel's wooden sword has a new origin: not an inn oar but a broken one from the boat, carved aboard.

mv716.text: In the novel, the boatman warns him: it's very late now.

mv718.text: Remember the letter's "when the time is right"? Here he only says:

mv720.text: Kojirō, for his part, accuses him to his face: late on purpose, every time.

mv721.text: As for that "said to be eighteen," even Yoshikawa says: surely not just eighteen.

mv722.text: This novel made "late on purpose" a story everyone knows.

mv723.text: Later someone told Yoshikawa: your Musashi is already a classic.

mv724.text: The version you first heard likely came from here.

mv725.text: But one witness in this file has said nothing all along. Who?

mv802.text: In the 10th month of 1643, aged 60, he climbed Higo's Mount Iwato and began The Book of Five Rings.

mv803.text: The preface ends: the 10th night of the 10th month, Tiger hour, he took up the brush.

mv804.text: The preface lists his record: a first win at thirteen, another at sixteen,

mv805.text: over sixty bouts in all, never once beaten, all between thirteen and twenty-eight or nine.

mv806.text: Recall the stone's number? His son's carving matches his own words.

mv807.text: By the Nitenki, he was 29 at Ganryūjima: the span's end.

mv809.text: The original reportedly burned; we checked a copy handed down by his disciples.

mv810.text: In this copy, Ganryū, Kojirō, Funashima: not one word.

mv811.text: The man who'd know best left nothing behind.

mv812.text: Think: he remembers his first opponent, yet leaves out his most famous duel. I won't guess why.

mv814.text: It also says the island back then was a sixth of its size today.

mv816.text: We think it, like the island, grew bigger later on.

mv817.text: Case closed: no firsthand record gives a motive; "on purpose" is a later reading.

mv818.text: As for what really happened on the island, accounts still differ.

mv820.text: Which manga or show first had him late on purpose? Tell me.

mv821.text: This channel only tells what the records hold. Subscribe to open files with us.
